entries.title: Seiya Suzuki’s defense: From ‘a little bit of a worry’ to highlight-reel throw, dependability for Cubs
entries.summary: <p>ST. LOUIS – If I say “Seiya Suzuki” and “defense,” what comes to your minds, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> fans?</p><p>Do you immediately jump to <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wJ5phrfmimM" target="_blank" >the fly ball he dropped in Atlanta</a> at the close of the 2023 season? Does it color your opinion of Suzuki as a defender?</p><p>Maybe Ivan Herrera is in the same camp. After all, the Cardinals catcher chose to take off for third base in the ninth inning Saturday night, likely not thinking Suzuki would throw him out with an on-the-money, highlight-reel chuck from right field.</p><p>But that’s what happened.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Seiya Suzuki makes a PERFECT throw to nab the runner at 3rd! 😮 <a href="https://t.co/GOk7JfB85x">pic.twitter.com/GOk7JfB85x</a></p>— MLB (@MLB) <a href="https://x.com/MLB/status/2060907385254752651?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">May 31, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p></p><p>Maybe it’s about time everyone – fans, opposing players, everyone – realized what kind of defender Suzuki can be.</p><p>“The last few years, with my defense, I think there was a little bit of worry,” Suzuki said through an interpreter following Saturday’s Cubs win. “But coming into this year, I felt good.”</p><p>He’s mostly looked good, too, at least to his teammates, who have noticed someone who has prioritized improving his defense.</p><p>“It’s never been an ability thing,” shortstop Dansby Swanson told the Sun-Times on Sunday. “I think Seiya might have more talent than anybody on our team. Just the things he’s capable of doing, it’s so impressive.</p><p>“For him to be almost humble enough to know he’s got things that he can work on and get better at – and also go work on them and get better at them – kind of shows who he is and how much he cares about his craft and being a good player.”</p><p>That’s a big deal, obviously, for a Cubs team that has built a reputation around playing sensational defense. Swanson is one of five Gold Glovers in the everyday lineup, alongside second baseman Nico Hoerner, third baseman Alex Bregman, left fielder Ian Happ and center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong.</p><p>But just because guys like Suzuki and first baseman Michael Busch aren’t award-winners for their defense doesn’t mean they’re not quality defenders.</p><p>After winning the team Gold Glove last season, the Cubs again rank as the best defensive team in baseball, according to multiple metrics like Outs Above Average and Fielding Run Value.</p><p>They’re flashing leather all over the field, and no opposing hitter or base-runner is safe.</p><p>“It really sets our team up to have a lot of success,” Swanson said, “because when you make other teams earn their way on base, earn their way around the bases, it can make it really, really hard. It can be like a suffocating type of feeling, just because all over the diamond, we have guys that are capable of doing some pretty special things.</p><p>“It is one of our calling cards of this group, our defensive ability.”</p><p>But as impressive as Saturday night’s throw was, as improved a defender as he’s become, Suzuki is here to hit.</p><p>Suzuki came into Sunday batting .250/.339/.405 with seven homers in 45 games. The batting average and on-base percentage actually look better than they did in 2025, but a middle-of-the-order hitter like Suzuki – who hit 32 bombs last year, two off the team lead – is expected to produce more in the power department.</p><p>“There’s good at-bats in there, some bad at-bats. But I think the amount of good at-bats are increasing, and I’m trying to figure everything out one at-bat at a time,” he said. “Even if I’m not hitting well, I can focus on defense and try to help the team there, too. But I’m trying to get that offense going.”</p><p>The total-package version of Suzuki is the kind of player the Cubs can use to achieve their sky-high, championship-level goals. And this might be their last chance to do so; Suzuki is due to hit free agency at the close of the campaign.</p><p>Until then, he’s a critical part of their winning formula – on both sides of the ball.</p>

entries.title: What can White Sox rookie David Sandlin do for an encore? How about a no-hitter?
entries.summary: <p>How on earth can White Sox right-hander <b>David Sandlin</b> top his major-league debut, in which he retired 18 consecutive hitters after allowing a leadoff home run?</p><p>‘‘Well, if he doesn’t throw a no-hitter, it might be a failure,’’ Sox pitching coach <b>Zach Bove</b> joked Sunday.</p><p>A no-no certainly would be an improvement, but not by a lot. Sandlin, a 6-4, 220-pounder with a fastball that reached 97.7 mph in the Sox’ 15-2 drubbing of the Twins on Wednesday, will see them again Monday, this time at Target Field.</p><p>Sandlin, 25, handled the Twins like a seasoned pro, allowing one hit — the homer to <b>Byron Buxton</b> — with four strikeouts and no walks in six innings. He threw only 61 pitches, 41 for strikes. And according to Elias, the 18 consecutive batters Sandlin retired were the most by a Sox pitcher in his major-league debut in the last, oh, 100 years.</p><p>‘‘It was great for him to have that success, especially in his debut,’’ Bove said. ‘‘But the next day is like, ‘What went well? What are some things we can do better?’ And then it’s on to the next week.</p><p>‘‘Obviously, he’s facing the same team, so we’re not going to overthink that. He’s kind of familiar with those guys; they’re familiar with him.’’</p><p>Something will have to give, but that hasn’t been a Sox starter lately. Since Sandlin’s debut, <b>Davis Martin</b>, <b>Anthony Kay</b> and <b>Sean Burke</b> allowed one run each in starts of five to six innings. In the other game, opener <b>Brandon Eisert</b> and <b>Erick Fedde</b> combined to allow two runs in 5⅓ innings.</p><h3>Schultz, Smith updates</h3><p>Rookie left-hander <b>Noah Schultz</b>, whom the Sox put on the 15-day injured list (retroactive to last Monday) with tendinitis in his right knee, threw well in the bullpen, Bove said.</p><p>‘‘We’ll see how he recovers and [do] another pen from there,’’ Bove said.</p><p>Bove said Schultz also is using the time to fix some things. He allowed 19 runs spanning 17⅓ innings in his last four starts before going on the IL.</p><p>‘‘We had this sample size at the major-league level with things that worked, with things that haven’t,’’ Bove said. ‘‘It’s a usage thing, No. 1. Specifically, with right-handed hitters, make sure that we’re throwing the right pitches. Working on a couple of the shapes, with his slider, adding a little depth to it. Those are the two big focuses.’’</p><p>Bove also said right-hander <b>Shane Smith</b>, who was the Sox’ Opening Day starter and is now on the IL at Triple-A Charlotte with a strained rotator cuff, resumed throwing last week.</p><h3>Notes</h3><p>The Sox put left-hander <b>Tyler Gilbert</b> on the family medical-emergency list and called up lefty <b>Chris Murphy</b>, keeping them with four left-handed relievers. The Sox put Murphy right to work, inserting him in the sixth inning Sunday. He walked three in 1⅓ innings but was bailed out by a double-play grounder and a pickoff that was scored as a caught-stealing.</p><p>• Infielder <b>Jacob Gonzalez</b>, the Sox’ first-round pick in 2023, became their 11th player to make his major-league debut this season. That’s tied for the second-most by a team before June since 1945, according to Elias. The Marlins had 12 before June in 1998.</p><h3>ON DECK</h3><p><b>SOX AT TWINS</b></p><p>Monday: David Sandlin (1-0, 1.50 ERA) vs. Joe Ryan (3-3, 2.94), 6:40 p.m., CHSN, 1000-AM.</p><p>Tuesday: Davis Martin (8-1, 2.00) vs. Connor Prielipp (1-3, 5.13), 6:40 p.m., CHSN, 1000-AM.</p><p>Wednesday: Erick Fedde (0-5, 5.40) vs. Taj Bradley (5-1, 3.21), 12:40 p.m., CHSN, 1000-AM.<br></p>

entries.title: White Sox put AL Central woes further behind them with sweep of Tigers
entries.summary: <p>The American League Central is a lovely division to travel through. No city is too far from the others.</p><p>For the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" >White Sox</a>, however, playing division rivals the last two years hasn’t been lovely at all.</p><p>In the miserable 2024 season, when the Sox lost a major-league-record 121 games, they went 10-42 against Central foes. They showed a modest improvement last season, going 18-34, but it was their fourth consecutive losing record in the division.</p><p>Look at them now.</p><p>After their 2-1 victory Sunday against the Tigers, the Sox are 11-3 in the division. The result gave them a sweep of the series, their second against a Central team, and came after they took three of four from the Twins.</p><p>You don’t need analytics to know a division title — and the accompanying playoff spot — go through a team’s division. And entering June, the Sox are only a game behind the first-place Guardians, the one division team they have yet to face.</p><p>‘‘These are games that we want,’’ said shortstop Colson Montgomery, who breathed life into a listless Sox offense with a solo home run in the seventh inning that tied the score.</p><p>To already have surpassed its Central victory total from 2024 shows how different this club is — not to mention how subpar the division is. But let’s focus on the Sox’ perspective.</p><p>‘‘Different team, different mindset,’’ Montgomery said. ‘‘We have all the confidence in the world. You gotta have that mindset that you can win, you can beat everybody.’’</p><p>They beat the Tigers on Sunday by seemingly waiting them out. After right-hander Keider Montero held them to two hits in six innings, the Sox exploited a Tigers bullpen that had blown a major-league-high 12 leads in the sixth inning or later.</p><p>‘‘We’ve shown all year that we’re a team that, if they get ahead, you can’t just stop,’’ Montgomery said. ‘‘We’re gonna be one at-bat away.’’</p><p>Montgomery’s homer came with one out against Drew Anderson, who subsequently got ripped for consecutive singles by Chase Meidroth, Jacob Gonzalez — whose first hit came in his big-league debut — and Tristan Peters, whose single put the Sox ahead.</p><p>‘‘I was looking for the changeup,’’ said Peters, who fouled off two fastballs and two curveballs before finally seeing that changeup. ‘‘He liked that pitch the other day when we faced him. I didn’t face him, but I was looking at other guys’ at-bats. So just trying to fight it off until I got my pitch.’’</p><p>The Sox’ bullpen had the opposite effect. After starter Sean Burke allowed one run in 5⅓ innings, Chris Murphy (who was called up Sunday), Brandon Eisert, Bryan Hudson and Tyler Davis combined to hold the Tigers to one hit the rest of the way. Davis earned his first career save. Closer Seranthony Dominguez had pitched in the last two games.</p><p>‘‘We learned last year with one-run games it’s not just about the bullpen; it’s about every phase of the game,’’ manager Will Venable said. ‘‘And as we’ve continued to progress in each of those departments, it’s all amounting to us having a better chance to win these closer games.’’</p><p>The Sox (32-27) are five games above .500 for the first time since Sept. 19, 2022, when they were 76-71. They won 18 games in May, their most in a month since May 2021, when they won 19 — and the Central.</p><p>While beating up on the teams below them is great, the Sox will need to maintain their edge when they finally face the Guardians in a series at Rate Field that begins June 22.</p><p>There’s still a lot of baseball to be played between now and then, including a brutal stretch against the Braves, Dodgers and Yankees. But by the looks of it, the Central is<br>becoming a lovely place for the Sox again.</p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" entries.title: Illinois lawmakers' fourth-down play to save Bears bill centers on publicly owned stadium
entries.summary: <p>SPRINGFIELD — Illinois lawmakers were improvising a desperation heave on Sunday to entice the Chicago Bears to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium" target="_blank" ><u>build a new dome</u></a> in their home state instead of Indiana, as the clock ticked down on the spring legislative session in Springfield.</p><p>The morning after top stadium negotiator and South Side state Sen. Bill Cunningham made the bombshell announcement his caucus <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/05/30/bears-stadium-bill-illinois-budget-deadline" target="_blank" ><u>wouldn’t support megaprojects property tax-incentive legislation</u></a> the team has sought for three years, officials were running a two-minute drill to come up with a completely new framework.</p><p>Sources close to the negotiations said the most promising idea was to allow municipalities to create their own stadium-financing authorities, akin to the Illinois Sports Facilities Authority that funded construction of what is now Rate Field, as well as the often-ridiculed 2003 renovation of Soldier Field.</p><p>That might provide the level playing field Senate Democrats have demanded in pitting Chicago against Arlington Heights — and any other Cook County municipality with at least 70,000 residents, and that might be inclined to throw public dollars at a stadium — for a new Bears dome.</p><p>Under the proposal — which was still in flux by the hour — the land and the stadium at whatever site the team picks would be owned by the municipality, whether it’s Arlington Heights, Chicago or another suitor.</p><p>The Bears would pay to build the stadium, but be completely off the hook for property taxes. That was their main concern in advocating for the tanked megaproject legislation, which would’ve allowed them to negotiate discounted payments in lieu of taxes (PILOT) in order to slash property tax bills the team has estimated would top $100 million in Arlington Heights.</p><p>"They would essentially pay for the stadium, enter an agreement with the municipality — could be any municipality — and the municipality would open the building," Cunningham said as the clock ticked Sunday evening. "I think all but three NFL stadiums are publicly owned right now, so it's a pretty common model."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure entries.title: Former Cubs CF Doug Glanville heaps praise on current CF Pete Crow-Armstrong
entries.summary: <p>ST. LOUIS — Doug Glanville has played center field. He has played for the Cubs. As one of the most thoughtful observers of baseball, he can offer an insider’s perspective on what it is to be Pete Crow-Armstrong.</p><p>‘‘I’ve had a lot of chances to talk to him,’’ Glanville said, sitting in the visitors’ dugout Sunday afternoon at Busch Stadium, while in town to serve as an analyst on ESPN’s radio broadcast of the Cubs-Cardinals game.</p><p>‘‘I’m always very impressed and blown away by his perspective that is well beyond his years. He just feels like somebody who has been around the block.</p><p>‘‘There’s a thoughtfulness to him, although he got in trouble recently because he’s also really emotional and plays that way. But even the way he described [the incident in Rate Field] on the back end, like how he has to be better, I’m more amazed at that.’’</p><p>Glanville was four years older than Crow-Armstrong when he made his big-league debut with the Cubs in 1996. Glanville was 25; Crow-Armstrong was 21 when he debuted in 2023.</p><p>Like Crow-Armstrong, Glanville was a first-round draft pick. He was taken 12th overall by the Cubs in 1991. Crow-Armstrong was taken by the Mets with the 19th pick overall in 2020. The comparisons end there, at least relative to their time with the Cubs. Glanville played one full season with the Cubs in 1997, then was traded that December to the Phillies for infielder Mickey Morandini.</p><p>It was only after he was traded to Philadelphia that Glanville became an everyday center fielder, where he was regarded as one of the best defenders in the league. But he never won a Gold Glove or was named to an All-Star team.</p><p>Crow-Armstrong, meanwhile, is already in his third full season with the Cubs after coming to Chicago in the Javy Baez deal. He has been an All-Star. He has won a Gold Glove. After signing a six-year, $115 million contract this spring, he already has lifetime financial security.</p><p>He is the face of the franchise.</p><p>‘‘I see why he’s the Pied Piper,’’ Glanville said, ‘‘because I think kids love him and he has that generational transcendent personality.</p><p>‘‘The passion, right? He could be anywhere, on the sandlots. He just wants to play. That’s like Prince going to a dive bar just to play.</p><p>‘‘When you become an oldhead, you want to see examples that the game you played is still here. There is an old-school to him that makes it feel like the game is still in good hands. There’s a purity to that. He deserves everything that people are saying about him.’’</p><p>Several days after the incident at the Rate, for which Crow-Armstrong was fined $5,000 for the vulgar language he directed at a woman who was taunting him from a ground-level section in the outfield, PCA made errors in consecutive games. Glanville has little doubt PCA’s mind was elsewhere.</p><p>‘‘Sure, and because of the standard he set by how he responded to it later, it should be,’’ Glanville said. ‘‘It will be because he cares about it. He knows that was not how he wanted to portray himself, and sometimes, yes, it carries out to the field.</p><p>‘‘Sometimes you just have bad days, for sure. But he knows the interconnection between what you call distraction or frustration or trying to balance this intensity with not going so far that you can’t focus. So that comes with the territory of someone who is outwardly passionate, and so you’re going to be outwardly upset, too.</p><p>‘‘I remember my dad had a stroke in 2000, and I was completely distracted. Like, I forgot how many outs there were. I was totally in another place. I get it.’’</p><p>On Saturday night, we all might have witnessed another way PCA can employ to respond to the vitriol he faces. He hit the longest home run of his career, a 444-foot blast, directly into the shirtless ‘‘Tarps Off’’ crowd chanting ‘‘Overrated’’ at him.</p><p>‘‘He’s freelancing, improvising; it’s just sort of the notes to play into the scene because that fires him up,’’ Glanville said. ‘‘To me, yesterday was a game that he kind of said, ‘OK, that’s another way to deal with it. There’s another way to challenge.’ ’’</p><p>That’s only one side of Glanville’s deep appreciation for Crow-Armstrong. There is also the kind of understanding that can exist between one master craftsman and another.</p><p>‘‘Talking center field with him is a joy,’’ Glanville said. ‘‘Like, how he thinks about his strengths and where he wants to start and comfort and jumps. How he understands what information to gather and what information to kind of discard or test.</p><p>‘‘I found his aptitude is off the charts, and then just watch his skill: the precision of his angles, his fearlessness at the wall, how he takes charge and how he’s gotten better.</p><p>‘‘The thing that I appreciate is, sometimes with metrics and analytics or data, people are like, ‘Give him the Gold Glove,’ before they even play 10 games. He’s leading those categories, but I feel like his excellence transcends the numbers.</p><p>‘‘I mean, those are measurable, for sure. But there’s something else, and I think that, to me, sustains him.’’<br></p><table class="cf wS" role="presentation" style="border-collapse: collapse;" id="rte-b0340690-5d5c-11f1-a23e-c3cf3bb33652"><tbody><tr><td colspan="1" rowspan="1" class="amq" style="margin: 0px; padding: 0px 16px; vertical-align: top; width: 44px; visibility: hidden;"></td><td colspan="1" rowspan="1" class="amr" style="margin: 0px; padding: 0px; width: 784px;"></td></tr></tbody></table>

entries.title: Man fatally shot in Douglas
entries.summary: <p>A man was shot and killed Sunday in the Douglas neighborhood on the South Side, police said.</p><p>The man, 23, was outside around 4:40 p.m. in the 2600 block of South Dearborn Street when someone fired shots, striking him in the chest and back, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The man was taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center in critical condition and later pronounced dead, authorities said.</p><p>No one is in custody, and detectives are investigating.</p>

entries.title: Side to side: Loss to Cardinals gives Cubs a worse record than White Sox
entries.summary: <p>ST. LOUIS — So what kind of odds do you suppose you could’ve gotten if you had strolled into the Cubby Bear a month ago and wagered that the White Sox would have a better record than the Cubs on June 1?</p><p>The Cubs began May with a 20-12 record, tied with the Reds for first place in the National League Central. The Sox were 15-17, their long-suffering fans pondering whether a .500 record might actually be within reach.</p><p>The Cubs already had a 10-game winning streak in their rearview mirror and were two victories into what would become another 10-game winning streak. The Sox were at least on the radar because of the emergence of their new slugger, <b>Munetaka Murakami</b>.</p><p>As they opened a series May 13 in Atlanta, the Cubs were alone in first place, 3½ games ahead of the field. The Sox were still under .500. And then things got messy for the Sons of <b>Craig Counsell</b>.</p><p>The Cubs lost 10 in a row. Their 5-1 loss to the Cardinals on Sunday night made it 12 losses in their last 15 games. They’re winless in their last seven series after dropping two of three to the Cards.</p><p>The Sox, despite losing Murakami to a hamstring injury, have won five straight. They’ve won their last two series, including a three-game sweep of the Tigers.</p><p>Check the standings. The Sox are 32-27. If the season ended today, they would be the second wild card. The Cubs are 32-28. If the season ended today, they would miss the playoffs.</p><p>If you’re a Cubs fan, you take your good news where you can get it. <b>Alex Bregman</b> hit a 404-foot home run in the sixth inning Sunday night, his third home run in 225 at-bats spanning 56 games. Bregman had promised the slug would come after he narrowly missed a home run Saturday. The Cubs can only hope.</p><p><b>June schedule filled with sub-.500 teams</b></p><p> With the Cubs’ messy May drawing to a close, the forecast for June couldn’t be more favorable.</p><p>Their next 22 games will be against teams with losing records — the Athletics, Giants, Rockies, Blue Jays and Mets. The A’s, who arrive at Wrigley Field on Tuesday for a three-game set, will be coming off a game in which they gave up 13 runs to the Yankees in the third inning, the Yanks’ biggest inning since 2005 and one shy of their record set in Babe Ruth’s first year as a Bomber. The five teams are a combined 41 games under .500.</p><p>The Cubs have home-and-home series against the Rockies and Giants, who follow the A’s into town this week, and play the Mets in New York later in the month, just before they face the division-leading Brewers in Milwaukee.</p><p>The Cubs’ rotation should soon be rejoined by left-hander <b>Matthew Boyd</b>, who made a strong rehab start Sunday for Triple-A Iowa in Indianapolis. Boyd, who has been out since May 4 with torn meniscus cartilage in his left knee, allowed only one run on <b>Rafael Flores’</b> triple in the second inning before being lifted after allowing two ground-ball singles to open the fifth.</p><p>Boyd threw 63 pitches, 41 for strikes, walking one and striking out two. Assuming he checks out OK on Monday, Boyd could return to the rotation this weekend against the Giants. Manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> wasn’t prepared to go that far Sunday, saying he had yet to see a report on Boyd’s outing.</p><p><b>PCA call</b></p><p><b>Eric Collins’</b> day job is play-by-play broadcaster for the NBA’s Hornets. On Saturday night, he was in the Fox booth, doing play-by-play of the Cubs-Cardinals game, part of his summer gig for the network. Here’s his call of <b>Pete Crow-Armstrong’s </b>444-foot home run:</p><p>“I think it’s bad intel, this ‘Overrated’ chant. He’s having a night. Look at this! P-C-A, right into the ‘Tarps Off’ row! Take that for ‘Overrated.’ Ha! That’s what talent does. It responds!’’</p><p><b>Brown keeps it in the yard</b></p><p>In the first game of the season, <b>Ben Brown </b>gave up a home run to the first batter he faced, <b>Jacob Young</b> of the Nationals. That was still when he was coming out of the bullpen for Counsell. That’s the only homer he has allowed. He has gone 51⅔ innings without allowing a homer in 16 appearances, including the five starts he has made since replacing Boyd in the Cubs’ rotation.</p><p>According to Cubs historian <b>Ed Hartig</b>, that’s the longest homerless streak by a Cubs pitcher since <b>Marcus Stroman’s </b>52⅔ innings in 2023. Brown was the team’s best reliever in two-inning stints and has been their best starter, as well. Overall, he has a 1.92 ERA, with 53 strikeouts and 15 walks.</p><p><b>Wicks takes his licks</b></p><p>Lefty <b>Jordan Wicks</b> got the quick hook from Counsell on Sunday night, lifted after allowing a leadoff single to <b>JJ Wetherholt</b> in the third inning. The first three Cardinals batters singled safely off Wicks, and two came around to score.</p><p>Wicks has made two starts since being called up after <b>Edward Cabrera </b>went on the 15-day injured list, and the numbers aren’t pretty: 7⅓ innings, 13 hits, 11 runs, 13.50 ERA.</p><p>Shaw to Iowa</p><p>Third baseman <b>Matt Shaw</b> is expected to be sent out on a rehab assignment to Iowa beginning Tuesday. He has been out since May 20 with tightness in his back.</p><p></p><p></p><table class="cf wS" role="presentation" style="border-collapse: collapse;" id="rte-4e04e3f0-5d56-11f1-9cd6-d329f37e8395"><tbody><tr><td colspan="1" rowspan="1" class="amq" style="margin: 0px; padding: 0px 16px; vertical-align: top; width: 44px; visibility: hidden;"></td><td colspan="1" rowspan="1" class="amr" style="margin: 0px; padding: 0px; width: 784px;"></td></tr></tbody></table>

entries.title: ‘Broadview 6’ defendants reflect on case doomed by feds' apparent misconduct: 'We didn’t commit a crime’
entries.summary: <p>There’s the “boring suburban dad,”<b> </b>whose children told him to stand up for what’s right.</p><p>The son of an immigrant, whose family already knew the sting of a federal prosecution.</p><p>A rising political disrupter, who says her progressive campaign was weighed down by bogus criminal charges. </p><p>And a campaign worker<b> </b>she calls her friend,<b> </b>and a “literal hero.”</p><p>They’re individuals. But together, they’re the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/05/21/broadview-ice-protest-grand-jury-transcript-kat-abughazaleh-trump" target="_blank" >four members of the “Broadview Six”</a><b> </b>who nearly faced trial this spring at the Dirksen Federal Courthouse — until the high-profile case against them collapsed amid claims of prosecutorial misconduct. The revelations <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/05/28/broadview-six-juliana-stratton-lori-lightfoot-andrew-boutros" target="_blank" >created a credibility crisis</a> for Chicago U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/05/27/broadview-six-boutros-kat-abughazaleh-ice-trump-chicago-broadview" target="_blank" >sent shockwaves across the country</a>.</p><p>They are former congressional candidate<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/04/02/kat-abughazaleh-political-future-campaign-hub-democratic-primary-loss-9th-congressional-district" target="_blank" >Kat<b> </b>Abughazaleh</a>, Oak Park village trustee Brian<b> </b>Straw, 45th Ward Democratic committeeperson Michael<b> </b>Rabbitt, and onetime Abughazaleh aide Andre<b> </b>Martin.</p><p>Finally free of the charges they faced for seven months, three of them agreed to speak with the Chicago Sun-Times after the case fell apart. They talked about the allegations against them, the legal theories surrounding it, and the price they paid for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/27/chicago-ice-trump-bovino-marimar-martinez-crime-border-patrol-midway-blitz" target="_blank" >another troubled prosecution of protesters</a> in Chicago that’s sure to find a place in the city’s history books.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/05/21/broadview-ice-protest-grand-jury-transcript-kat-abughazaleh-trump" target="_blank" >‘Broadview Six’ charges dropped as Chicago’s top federal prosecutor admits case was tainted by misconduct</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Now that they’re also free to speak to each other, Rabbitt said they share a “very special bond.”</p><p>They’ve had to raise money to pay legal bills. Abughazaleh said she and Martin faced bankruptcy. Rabbitt<b> </b>worried<b> </b>about being detained when he arrived home from overseas.<b> </b>And Straw called it a “living hell for me and my family.”</p><p>That includes Straw's young children, who he said “had nightmares related to this case.”</p><p>Six people <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/10/29/kat-abughazaleh-conspiracy-indictment-broadview-protests-donald-trump-deportation-campaign" target="_blank" >originally faced charges</a>, hence the “Broadview Six” moniker. Most are involved in local Democratic politics. Also charged were former Cook County Board candidate Catherine<b> </b>“Cat”<b> </b>Sharp<b> </b>and<b> </b>musician<b> </b>Joselyn<b> </b>Walsh, but their charges were <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/12/chicago-midway-blitz-immigration-trump-kat-abughazaleh-sharp-joselyn-walsh-broadview-six" target="_blank" >dropped in March</a>.</p><p>Prosecutors accused the six of a felony<b> </b>conspiracy<b> </b>for being part of a crowd on Sept. 26 whose members surrounded<b> </b>an immigration agent’s SUV<b> </b>and pushed, scratched<b> </b>and otherwise damaged it. Later, prosecutors sought to put the final four defendants <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/04/29/broadview-ice-crime-chicago-trump-kat-abughezaleh" target="_blank" >on trial<b> </b>for misdemeanors</a>.</p><p>None of the six defendants were ever specifically accused of causing damage to the SUV. The feds later argued<b> </b>the conspiracy was<b> </b>“spontaneous.”</p><p>Boutros defended the case, even after permanently<b> </b>dismissing<b> </b>the charges May 21. He said the behavior by the six and others in September during an Operation Midway Blitz protest was “unacceptable in a civilized society.”</p><p>But Abughazaleh said, “I think my conduct fits very well in a civilized society.</p><p>“A society where we get to dissent from the government, and we expect our rights to be respected,” she said. “I think that is extremely civilized conduct.”</p><p>They have stories to tell.<b> </b>About how Straw pressed legal issues in court when others might have given in. How Rabbitt confronted the trauma of his father’s<b> </b>federal<b> </b>prosecution<b> </b>in Missouri. And how Abughazaleh ran a political campaign while under indictment.</p><p>But their tales overlap — outside<b> </b>a suburban immigration<b> </b>facility, inside a courtroom in Chicago and in a common pursuit of justice in what comes next.</p><p>They noted they’ve each, independently, already taken a stand against the Justice Department.</p><p>“At any point, any of us could have taken a deal,” Abughazaleh said.</p><p>“And none of us did.”</p><h3><b>A protest prompts charges</b></h3><p>They first gathered together on a sunny<b> </b>September<b> </b>morning<b> </b>in the western suburb of Broadview, home to a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/10/01/broadview-immigration-processing-center-detention-ice-dhs" target="_blank" >U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement holding facility</a> that became a hotbed for protests during Midway Blitz.</p><p>Many of the people detained during the deportation campaign wound up inside the facility. A federal judge would later hear testimony about people being crammed into a holding cell there<b> </b>100 at a time, with nowhere to sleep but a dirty floor near an open toilet.</p><p>Rabbitt and Straw said they went to protest there for the first time Sept. 26. But Abughazaleh, in the midst of her congressional campaign, had already made news there<b> </b>with an infamous video of a federal agent <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/09/19/ice-broadview-protest-write-thru" target="_blank" >tossing her to the ground</a>.</p><p>The protesters engaged that morning in what’s known as a Jericho Walk, court records show. It’s a form of protest with spiritual roots. Though Broadview police purportedly helped clear a path through the crowd so other vehicles could pass through, court filings say an ICE agent decided<b> </b>to roll his SUV slowly through the gathering around 7:45 a.m.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/10/29/kat-abughazaleh-conspiracy-indictment-broadview-protests-donald-trump-deportation-campaign" target="_blank" >Feds charge Kat Abughazaleh, other political candidates in indictment tied to Broadview protests</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Federal prosecutors alleged that the protesters,<b> </b>including the six who would be accused in the indictment, “swarmed the government vehicle” to keep the agent from going to work.</p><p>The “Broadview Six” saw it differently. Straw said he was “shocked to see a large SUV driving into a crowd of people.”<b> </b>Rabbitt said he was “stunned and alarmed.”<b> </b>Abughazaleh said her mind went back to a moment one week earlier, when she’d helped a fallen man whose head wound up in front of a car tire. She worried something like that could happen again — with fatal results.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a But in a sign of things to come, Straw attorney Christopher Parente<b> </b>objected<b> </b>to Straw having to turn over his passport.</p><p>It’s a standard condition of release for a defendant awaiting trial. It’s a theory based on proximity and parallel action, which simply is no basis for a charge of conspiracy.”</p><p>“From the start, we just had concerns over how it was possible that a grand jury could indict a conspiracy charge based on what had actually happened in this case,” Straw added.</p><p>Defense attorneys <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/05/04/broadview-six-grand-jury-transcript-conspiracy" target="_blank" >sought transcripts of the grand jury proceedings</a> as the case moved forward before U.S. District Judge<b> </b>April<b> </b>Perry. my late father, and all the great things he accomplished in his life,”<b> </b>Michael Rabbitt said. “And the fact that he, in the history books, is defined by one thing that happened to him, his conviction, and yet I had to reflect on, ‘What does this mean for me?’”</p><p>Given that Michael Rabbitt’s protest and indictment revolved around <a class="Link" target="_blank" >the Trump administration’s deportation campaign</a>, he said he’s also been thinking about his mother, an immigrant from Ireland,<b> </b>as well as his mother-in-law, an immigrant from Poland.</p><p>“The cause of immigrants is important to us,” he said, “and the history of immigration here in Chicago, of course, is so important.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" into hiding when indicted by the U.S. attorney’s office. Instead, Abughazaleh announced her indictment on social media.</p><p>“I wanted to be able to tell my own story and not have it told for me,” she said.</p><p>“And I don’t trust the government to tell that story honestly,” she added.</p><p>By the time of the indictment, Abughazaleh had become a high-profile Democratic candidate in the crowded 9th congressional district primary race. She ultimately <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/03/17/us-house-illinois-9th-congressional-district-primary-results" target="_blank" >came in second<b> </b>for the nomination<b> </b>won by Biss</a>.</p><p>On the surface, it seemed the indictment from the Trump Justice Department might have given her campaign a boost. She certainly didn’t shy away from it.</p><p>“What else are you supposed to do but embrace it?” she asked.</p><p>“Because it’s happening,” Abughazaleh said. “And I’m not ashamed of being a target by this administration.”</p><p>She said “it definitely hurt the campaign,”<b> </b>though.</p><p>“It takes resources,” she said. “We had to pay legal bills. … Every single piece of communication that went out, we had to run by our lawyers. That costs money.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/04/02/kat-abughazaleh-political-future-campaign-hub-democratic-primary-loss-9th-congressional-district" target="_blank" >After primary loss, Kat Abughazaleh moves to boost campaigns across Midwest</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>There’s also the strain of being under indictment, which didn’t only affect her. Martin, a member of her campaign staff, had also been indicted. Abughazaleh called Martin a “friend” and<b> </b>“literal hero”<b> </b>who is “braver than anyone I know.”</p><p>“Two people on our staff were indicted by the federal government, and we still had to act like normal,”<b> </b>Abughazaleh said. “And it’s really hard. It’s so stressful.”</p><p>In fact, she said facing prosecution amid a political campaign “was one of the most excruciating things of my life.” One of her goals now is to prevent what happened to the “Broadview Six” from happening to others.</p><p>She said it could happen to anyone, and it’s OK to be afraid. She’s “afraid all the time,” she said.</p><p>“But we all have a lot of courage, especially here in Chicago,” Abughazaleh said.<b> </b>“And courage isn’t doing something because you’re unafraid. It’s doing something despite being afraid.”</p><p>And, she said, “we had nothing to apologize for.”</p><p>“We didn’t commit a crime. We were the victims. And we refused to let the government paint us as anything else.”</p>

entries.title: Dirty soda trend finds a home at Lake View shop
entries.summary: <p>Syed Ahmed's longtime sweet tooth led him to open Chicago's first dirty soda shop, Johnny's Dirty Soda and Snacks.</p><p>Dirty soda — a customized iced drink mixing soda, flavored creams, syrups or fruit — has grown in popularity thanks to the Hulu reality TV show "The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives," which follows a group of Mormon mom influencers. The show had fans eagerly scoping out what dirty soda combinations the stars were ordering.</p><p>“My younger self would’ve loved this,” said Ahmed, a Chicago native. “I’ve had like five or six root canals from eating sugar.”</p><p>Dirty sodas are a well-known aspect of Mormon, and Utah, culture. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints prohibits members from drinking alcohol or coffee, making dirty soda an acceptable alternative for members.</p><p>U.S. alcohol consumption hit its <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/food-drink/2025/12/03/chicago-is-a-drinkers-paradise-even-for-the-sober-and-the-sober-curious-among-us" target="_blank" >lowest point in 90 years</a>, a 2024 Gallup survey found. And Gen Z and millennials are spending less on alcohol because of changing tastes — not because of higher liquor prices, according to a February report from Bank of America Institute.</p><p>Chains like Utah-based Swig have been serving dirty sodas for decades, mostly out West. Now, fast-food businesses are getting into the dirty soda trend, too. </p><p>McDonald's rolled out a new line of refreshers and craft sodas in May. The six specialty drinks include Dirty Dr. Pepper, with vanilla and cold foam, and Orange Dream, pairing Hi-C Orange Lavaburst with vanilla and cold foam.</p><p>Dunkin' has come out with Dunkin' Dirty Soda, which combines coffee milk with Pepsi and sweet cold foam.</p><p>And Taco Bell made its Dirty Sips — including Mountain Dew Baja Blast dirty soda — part of its permanent menu. </p><p>Ahmed discovered dirty soda shops on a trip to Arizona in 2024 — the year “The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives” premiered. </p><p>“I went to one of these soda shops, and I'm, like, ‘Dude, this is amazing. ... I wish they had something like this in the Midwest,’ ” he said.</p><p>Back home in Chicago, he encouraged his family to get in on the business and opened Johnny's with his sister Sheena Ahmed, brother-in-law Saleh "Johnny" Ewaida and Saleh's brother Omar Ewaida.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a entries.title: Evanston novelist Daniel Kraus says his biggest fear is dying before he can write it all down
entries.summary: <p>After you’ve read Daniel Kraus’ gorgeous, frequently grotesque novel “Angel Down,” which barrels in a single sentence across the corpse-clogged battlefields of World War I France, a question might come to mind — once you’re again on solid ground and your ears have stopped ringing: How the hell does Kraus come up with this stuff?</p><p>“And the sky is slashed with yellow howitzer shot revealing body parts in the stew through which they squirm, two severed arms holding hands, boots still potted with feet, a set of shoulders that dangles a curtain of hairy chest, nothing alive here but opportunistic animals, a stoat dragging away a complete digestive system, a blackbird perched atop an opened head to peck at the brains,” Kraus writes in one passage early in the book.</p><p>Kraus recently won the 2026 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction for the novel. The man who calls Evanston home taps into a cavernous reservoir of stomach-churning, astonishing imagery in “Angel Down” and, happily for his fans, a wellspring in no danger of running dry.</p><p>“I don’t ever really get writer’s block,” Kraus said, chatting with the Chicago Sun-Times last week. “My issue with writing is that I’m going to die before I get everything out. I have so many books I want to write.”</p><p>Kraus is among the headliners at this year’s American Writers Festival, featuring some 90 writers June 6 at the American Writers Museum (180 N. Michigan Ave.) and June 7 at the Harold Washington Library Center (400 S. State St.). Kraus is appearing with writer Susan Orlean at noon June 7, at the library center. The two will be discussing cinematic adaptations of their work.</p><p>The festival is free and seats are available first come, first served. Previous headliners have included Viet Thanh Nguyen, who won the 2016 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction with his debut novel “The Sympathizer,” and screenwriter and filmmaker Aaron Sorkin.</p><p>Writing is “just like breathing” for Kraus. So the last few weeks have felt like a caffeine junkie denied his morning fix.</p><p>“My schedule has been swallowed up,” he said of his post-Pulitzer life. “I’m appreciative of it, but it’s a lot. Without going into specifics, it has changed everything almost overnight.”</p><p>The Pulitzer jury described “Angel Down” as “a breathless novel …, a stylistic tour-de-force that blends such genres as allegory, magical realism and science fiction into a cohesive whole, told in a single sentence.”</p><p>Like “1917,” director Sam Mendes’ one-shot 2019 movie (also set on the cratered battlefields of World War I), Kraus’ single-sentence approach works to evoke the unrelenting horror and nowhere-to-hide nature of trench warfare.</p><h3>Horror as childhood escape </h3><p>In “Angel,” five U.S. Army misfits are dispatched to silence the “shriek” of a fallen, fatally wounded comrade somewhere in the “black world hulking beneath the slow cyclones of smoke.” What they find instead is a shrieking real-life angel ensnared in barbed wire. For much of the novel, the angel is mute and just glints of blinding light — a creature impossible to see in any detail.</p><p>“The angel in ‘Angel Down’ works like the zombies in ‘Night of the Living Dead,’ or it works like a lot of episodes of ‘The Twilight Zone,’ where it’s a catalyst. It’s there mostly for the characters to reveal themselves,” Kraus said. “They are sort of like time bombs that were going to go off at some point, and this is the thing that pulls the pin of their grenades.”</p><p>Kraus grew up in Fairfield, Iowa, a place of wide open spaces dotted with farmhouses, a landscape he found isolating.</p><p>“The short version is that horror media, beginning with ‘Night of the Living Dead’ and ‘The Twilight Zone,’ was a way of mastering my fear and anxiety against a world I found threatening. Watching horror became a way of building a suit of armor, film by film, novel by novel,” he said.</p><p>The urgency to write took hold in first grade. He and a buddy drew crayon monsters, which led to stories about them in combat.</p><p>“Then I never stopped,” Kraus said. “In middle school, I was writing what would essentially be novellas.”</p><p>He began writing novels in high school. Some three decades later, Kraus, 50, is the best-selling author of 28 books, from horror to science fiction to young adult. He co-authored two novels with filmmaker Guillermo del Toro, including “The Shape of Water,” which went on to become an Oscar-winning movie.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div You might find Kraus at Reprise Coffee Roasters or Sketchbook Brewing Company, he said. A book on the big screen in which human flesh is filleted, fried and in every imaginable way mutilated?</p><p>“This feels a lot more possible than ‘Whalefall’ did,” Kraus said of his 2023 novel that has been made into a soon-to-be-released movie. “That’s a book about someone stuck in a whale stomach. entries.title: Illinois Democrats pass $56B state budget that includes new taxes on prediction markets, crypto
entries.summary: <p>SPRINGFIELD — Debating into the early hours of Monday during an overtime finish to their spring session, Illinois lawmakers passed a nearly $56 billion state budget early Monday to increase food assistance in the wake of federal funding cuts without burdening “everyday working families," according to supermajority Democrats who control Springfield. </p><p>The plan rolls in new taxes on the burgeoning industries of prediction markets, cryptocurrency and fantasy sports, while also dinging digital advertising revenue. </p><p>Budget leaders aren't yet counting on revenue from all the controversial new levies, which are near certain to face legal challenges — but they are banking on some $200 million from a tax on social media companies similar to the one facing <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/03/13/chicago-social-media-tax-lawsuit-facebook-tiktok-block-brandon-johnson" >a court challenge in Chicago</a>. </p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/05/31/bears-stadium-bill-springfield-arlington-heights-hammond-indiana" >Bears blocked in Illinois: House spikes late-session play for new stadium bill that cleared Senate</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Other fiscal moves intended to make ends meet in a tight budget year include a redirection of sales tax revenue on sugary beverages to the state’s general fund instead of to capital projects, according to state Rep. Robyn Gabel, an Evanston Democrat and top budget negotiator.</p><p>“We've constructed a budget that meets people's most pressing needs, including key investments that allow Illinois to move forward in areas where Washington has chosen to retreat,” Gabel said. ”The uncertainty in Washington and the resulting affordability crisis facing families has emphasized our need to be surgical and our approach to building this budget.”</p><p>But a coalition of progressive Democrats said the plan didn’t do enough “to fully fund quality education, accessible healthcare and reliable public services for every Illinoisan."</p><p>And Republicans, boxed out of budget negotiations as usual in Democrat-controlled Springfield, decried the increase from last year's $55.2 billion budget and the new taxes.</p><p>“They're loading up their grocery cart literally before they have any idea how much they're going to spend,” said state Sen. Chapin Rose, a top GOP budget negotiator from downstate Mahomet.</p><p>The last in the series of taxing and spending bills that comprise the budget wasn't approved until 4:13 a.m. Monday, when the spending end of the proposal passed the House by a vote of 76-39, after clearing the Senate 37-21. </p><p>The yearly budget crunch was unfolding at the same time that many lawmakers were <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/05/31/bears-stadium-bill-springfield-arlington-heights-hammond-indiana" ><u>furiously working to craft new legislation to entice the Chicago Bears</u></a> to build a new stadium in Illinois instead of Indiana.</p><p>A first draft of the 3,500-plus page spending plan was unveiled with barely a day left in the legislative session, a proposal that largely aligned with the maintenance budget Gov. JB Pritzker proposed earlier this year amid troubling economic headwinds and federal funding cuts under President Donald Trump.</p><p>“There are no tax increases on everyday working families,” said state Sen. Elgie Sims, D-Chicago.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>John O’Connor/AP</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Property tax relief</h3><p>As lawmakers tried to address the Bears’ property tax concerns, they also tried to do so for average homeowners by re-funding a property tax relief program that was left out of last year’s budget. Since property taxes are levied by school boards and local taxing bodies to make up for funding that doesn’t come from the state, school districts that need more funds can apply for additional state funding to help keep a lid on local property taxes, Sims said.</p><p>With Democrats nationwide underscoring affordability issues heading into a pivotal midterm election, Sims said the state would suspend a scheduled 1.3-cent-per-gallon increase in the gas tax, and implement a sales tax holiday on school supplies.</p><p>The spending plan retains a $143 million health care program for older immigrants without documentation, and $4 million for immigrant welcoming service centers.</p><p>And with new federal work requirements pending for SNAP recipients, the budget carves out $70 million for a new program named Families Receiving Emergency Support for Hunger, or FRESH.</p><p>“We are facing a crisis,” Sims said. “There are over 100,000 individuals who will lose SNAP benefits as a result of the actions from our hostile federal government.”</p><p>The FRESH program offers one-time $400 individual payments to families who were recently booted from the SNAP program.</p><h3>Raises for state legislators</h3><p>State lawmakers are in line for 3% cost-of-living raises tied to inflation, as outlined by state law, raising their base salaries to $101,450.</p><p>The budget partially relies on extra state revenue brought in from sales tax on motor fuel in the last few months as a result of skyrocketing gas prices. The additional $150 million wasn’t anticipated by the governor when he first proposed a budget in February, so lawmakers redirected the excess funds to plug other holes.</p><p>Rose pushed back on the “surplus on sales tax for motor fuel,” saying “there is no surplus. We’re gouging these people because of what is happening with the price of gas.”</p><p>And in another rare Springfield win for Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson — along with the scuttling of the Bears’ Arlington Heights legislation — lawmakers restored funding to local governments’ cut of state income tax back to 6.47%, over the Pritzker-proposed 6.23%.</p><p>The governor's proposal would have cost municipalities an estimated $60 million annually, including $12.7 million for Chicago alone, according to data from the Illinois Municipal League. Johnson had joined numerous other mayors in Springfield <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/05/06/mayor-brandon-johnson-local-government-funding-cuts-jb-pritzker-springfield-trip" target="_blank" ><u>earlier this month</u></a> to protest the governor's proposed shift.</p><h3>Cellphone ban in schools</h3><p>In the waning hours of session, a series of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/illinois-governor/2026/05/02/jb-pritzker-build-initiative-affordable-housing-plan-municipalities-concerns" target="_blank" ><u>housing initiatives</u></a> prioritized by Pritzker went mostly unaddressed. But after passing regulations on artificial intelligence and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/05/28/auto-home-insurance-reform-illinois-general-assembly-passage" target="_blank" ><u>insurance companies</u></a> last week, the governor scored another long-awaited legislative win with a ban on cellphones in schools.</p><p>The statewide school ban was first proposed by the governor in early 2025, but it failed to make it through both chambers. It'll get a signature from Pritzker, adding Illinois to a growing list of states trying to take cellphones out of the classroom.</p><p>“Every parent and educator knows the damage that unchecked screen time and social media can do to our children and how disruptive they can be in school,” Pritzker said in a statement. “The bipartisan support for this effort reflects the urgency educators and families across Illinois feel.”</p>
